title: A Federal Judge Just Killed Trump's $100,000 H-1B Fee. The Rest of the Crackdown Is Just Getting Started.
excerpt: The ruling is a win for tech companies and Indian workers — but a wave of site visits, RFEs, and revocations means the H-1B system is still under siege.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • A federal judge struck down a $100,000 fee on H-1B visa petitions, benefiting tech firms and Indian workers.
  • Indian nationals received 72% of all H-1B visas approved in fiscal year 2025.
  • H-1B denial rates have risen to approximately 12% in early FY2026, with higher rates for IT services companies.
  • USCIS has resumed issuing Notices of Intent to Revoke for previously approved H-1B petitions.
  • Indian H-1B holders face estimated green card wait times of 50-80 years due to per-country caps.
A federal judge in Northern California has struck down the Trump administration's proposed $100,000 fee for certain H-1B visa petitions, calling it "arbitrary and capricious" in a ruling that hands the tech industry and immigrant workers a significant — but potentially temporary — victory. Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California issued the decision on July 8, siding with a coalition of tech companies, universities, and immigration advocacy groups that had challenged the fee as an unlawful attempt to price skilled workers out of the visa system. But immigration attorneys say the celebration should be measured. The fee was just one front in a multi-pronged offensive against the H-1B program that shows no signs of slowing down. ## What the Fee Was In March 2026, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services published a final rule imposing a new "Fraud Prevention and Detection Fee" of $100,000 on H-1B petitions filed by companies where more than 50% of employees are on H-1B or L-1 visas — a threshold that primarily targets Indian IT outsourcing firms like Infosys, Wipro, TCS, and HCLTech. The fee was framed as necessary to fund expanded fraud investigations. Critics called it a backdoor ban. At $100,000 per petition — on top of existing fees that can already exceed $10,000 — the economics of sponsoring an H-1B worker would become untenable for many employers. "This wasn't a fee. It was a wall built out of dollar signs," said Greg Siskind, a Memphis-based immigration attorney who filed an amicus brief in the case. ## The Ruling Judge Corley's 47-page opinion dismantled the government's justification on multiple grounds. The court found that USCIS had failed to provide adequate notice-and-comment opportunity, had not demonstrated a rational connection between the fee amount and actual fraud prevention costs, and had applied the fee in a discriminatory manner by targeting a specific subset of employers. "The agency's own data shows that fraud rates among H-1B-dependent employers are not materially different from the general H-1B population," Corley wrote. "A fee structure that imposes a 1,000% surcharge on a subset of petitioners based on workforce composition, without evidence of proportionally higher fraud, is the definition of arbitrary." The ruling issues a nationwide injunction, meaning USCIS cannot collect the fee from any employer while the case is on appeal. The Department of Justice is expected to appeal to the Ninth Circuit. ## Why It Matters for Indian Workers The numbers tell the story. Indian nationals received approximately 72% of all H-1B visas approved in fiscal year 2025, according to USCIS data. The companies most directly targeted by the $100,000 fee — large IT services firms — employ tens of thousands of Indian workers in the United States. Had the fee taken effect, industry analysts estimated it would have reduced H-1B filings by Indian IT companies by 30-40%, effectively stranding thousands of workers who were expecting visa renewals or transfers. "For a mid-level engineer at an IT services company making $95,000 a year, a $100,000 fee makes the math impossible for the employer," said Lynden Melmed, a former USCIS chief counsel now in private practice. "The worker doesn't lose a fee — they lose a job, a visa, and potentially their ability to stay in the country." ## The Bigger Picture: Enforcement by a Thousand Cuts Immigration attorneys warn that the fee ruling, while important, addresses only the most visible element of a broader strategy to constrict H-1B usage. **Site visits have surged.** USCIS's Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate has dramatically increased unannounced worksite visits in 2026. Attorneys report visits happening within days of petition filing — before adjudication — with investigators asking detailed questions about job duties, reporting structures, and whether the work matches the petition description. **Requests for Evidence (RFEs) are at record levels.** Data compiled by the National Foundation for American Policy shows that RFE rates for H-1B petitions exceeded 45% in the first quarter of FY2026, up from roughly 30% in FY2024. RFEs add months to processing times and often require expensive legal responses.

**Denial rates are climbing.** After falling during the Biden administration, H-1B denial rates have risen to approximately 12% in early FY2026, with significantly higher rates for IT services companies. Some specialty occupation categories — particularly entry-level IT consulting roles — are seeing denial rates above 25%. **Visa revocations are back.** In a practice largely dormant since 2020, USCIS has resumed issuing Notices of Intent to Revoke (NOIRs) for previously approved H-1B petitions, particularly for workers on assignment at third-party client sites. This is especially alarming for Indian IT workers, many of whom work in consulting arrangements. ## The Green Card Shadow Underlying all of this is the decades-long green card backlog that affects Indian nationals more than any other group. With per-country caps limiting India to roughly 7% of employment-based green cards despite representing the majority of applicants, Indian H-1B holders face estimated wait times of 50-80 years for permanent residency. This means that unlike H-1B holders from most other countries — who can typically obtain a green card within 1-3 years — Indian workers remain on temporary visas for their entire careers, vulnerable to every policy shift, every fee increase, and every enforcement action. "The cruelty is structural," said Kelli Durkin, co-founder of Immigration Voice, an advocacy group. "You bring people in on a temporary visa, make them wait a lifetime for permanent status, and then change the rules every four years. It's not a system — it's a trap." ## What Happens Next The government is expected to appeal Judge Corley's ruling. The Ninth Circuit could take 12-18 months to decide, and the case could eventually reach the Supreme Court if the circuit courts split. In the meantime, the other enforcement mechanisms — site visits, RFEs, denials, revocations — continue unabated. Congress, despite bipartisan acknowledgment that the H-1B system needs reform, remains gridlocked on immigration legislation. For the estimated 600,000 Indian nationals currently on H-1B visas in the United States, the ruling offers relief on one front while the broader landscape remains hostile. The $100,000 fee is dead — for now. But the system it was designed to break was already breaking under the weight of its own contradictions. *Sources: U.S. District Court, Northern District of California (Case No. 3:26-cv-02841), National Foundation for American Policy, USCIS quarterly data, Reuters, Bloomberg Law*
